qs.q: In 2019, how many Indian students went abroad?
qs.p: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it. The number of Indian students going abroad for higher studies has increased by 68.79 per cent in the past year, according to data provided by the Minister of State in the Ministry of Education, Subhas Sarkar. As per the data provided by him in the Lok Sabha, the number of Indians enrolled in foreign varsities increased from 4.44 lakh in 2021 to 7.5 lakh in 2022. He clarified that while the Bureau of Immigration and Ministry of Home Affairs maintain departure and arrival data of Indians, there is no index for capturing the category of Indians going abroad for higher education. “Purpose of Indians going abroad for higher education is captured manually based either on their verbal disclosure or the type of visa of the destination country produced by them at the time of immigration clearance,” Sarkar said. According to the data provided by the ministry, the number of Indian nationals increased from 4.54 lakh in 2017 to 5.17 lakh in 2018. There was a significant increase in 2019 as well, with 5.86 lakh students flying out of the country. However, during the Covid pandemic, the number of Indian nationals in foreign varsities saw a drastic dip as only 2.59 lakh students were registered. While the number continued to remain low, it saw a slight increase in 2021 with 4.44 lakh registrations. However, the number has significantly jumped to 7.5 lakh in 2022. The increase in the number of Indian nationals abroad corresponds with the latest immigration reports from some of the popular study-abroad destinations such as the US, UK, and Australia. For the UK, the Immigration Statistics Report states that 127,731 visas were granted to Indian students in September 2022, an increase of 93,470 (+273 per cent) against 34,261 in 2019. Similarly, in the US, the number of Indian students has more than doubled, and the Open Doors Report 2022 has predicted that the number of Indian students heading to America is likely to surpass those from China in 2022-23.

qs.p: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. We sit in the last row, bumped about but free of stares. The bus rolls out of the dull crossroads of the city, and we are soon in the open countryside, with fields of sunflowers as far as the eye can see, their heads all facing us. Where there is no water, the land reverts to the desert. While still on level ground, we see in the distance the tall range of the Mount Bogda, abrupt like a shining prism laid horizontally on the desert surface. It is over 5,000 metres high, and the peaks are under permanent snow, in powerful contrast to the flat desert all around. Heaven lake lies part of the way up this range, about 2,000 metres above sea level, at the foot of one of the highest snow-peaks. As the bus climbs, the sky, brilliant before, grows overcast. I have brought nothing warm to wear. It is all down at the hotel in Urumqi. Rain begins to fall. The man behind me is eating overpoweringly smelly goat’s cheese. The bus window leaks inhospitably but reveals a beautiful view. We have passed quickly from the desert through arable land to pasture and the ground is now green with grass, the slopes dark with pine. A few cattle drink at a clear stream flowing past moss-covered stones; it is a Constable landscape. The stream changes into a white torrent, and as we climb higher I wish more and more that I had brought with me something warmer than the pair of shorts that have served me so well in the desert. The stream (which, we are told, rises in Heaven Lake) disappears, and we continue our slow ascent. About noon, we arrive at Heaven Lake, and look for a place to stay at the foot, which is the resort area. We get a room in a small cottage, and I am happy to note that there are thick quilts on the bed. Standing outside the cottage, we survey our surroundings. Heaven Lake is long, sardine- shaped and fed by snowmelt from a stream at its head. The lake is an intense blue, surrounded on all sides by green mountain walls, dotted with distant sheep. At the head of the lake, beyond the delta of the inflowing stream, is a massive snow-capped peak which dominates the vista; it is part of a series of peaks that culminate, a little out of view, in Mount Bogda itself. For those who live in the resort, there is a small mess-hall by the shore. We eat here sometimes, and sometimes buy food from the vendors outside, who sell kabab and naan until the last buses leave. The kababs, cooked on skewers over charcoal braziers, are particularly good; highly spiced and well-done. Horse’s milk is available too from the local Kazakh herdsmen, but I decline this. I am so affected by the cold that Mr. Cao, the relaxed young man who runs the mess, lends me a spare pair of trousers, several sizes too large but more than comfortable. Once I am warm again, I feel a pre-dinner spurt of energy—dinner will be long in coming—and I ask him whether the lake is good for swimming in.

qs.p: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it. From January 28 to February 4, 2023, a Chinese-operated, large white high-altitude balloon was seen in North American airspace, including Alaska, western Canada, and the contiguous United States. The American and Canadian militaries asserted that the balloon was for surveillance, while the Chinese government maintained it was a civilian meteorological research airship that had been blown off course. Analysts said that the balloon's flight path and structural characteristics made it dissimilar from those which have typically been used for meteorological research. The U.S. Department of State said that the balloon was capable of locating electronic communication devices, including mobile phones and radios, and that American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft deployed to track the balloon in the air revealed that the balloon carried antennas and other equipment "clearly for intelligence surveillance and inconsistent with the equipment on board weather balloons." The State Department said that the spy balloon was part of a global Chinese military-directed surveillance effort in which Chinese spy balloons have flown over more than 40 nations in five continents. On February 4, the U.S. Air Force shot down the balloon over U.S. territorial waters off the coast of South Carolina, on the order of U.S. President Joe Biden. Debris from the wreckage was recovered and sent to the FBI Laboratory in Quantico, Virginia, for analysis. The incident increased U.S.-China tensions. The incident prompted U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken to delay a diplomatic visit to Beijing, which was set to be his first since 2018. It also further strained Canada–China relations, as Canada summoned the Chinese ambassador because of the violation of Canadian airspace. On February 3, the U.S. Department of Defense announced that a second Chinese balloon was passing over Latin America, which China also said belonged to it. On February 10, the Air Force shot down another aerial object over U.S. territory at the order of President Biden.

C|Computer Fundamentals & CPU.why: Computer fundamentals is the largest Computer Knowledge topic in Tier 2, at about 3.2 of the 20 questions per paper across CGL 2022 to CGL 2025 (4.25 in 2022, 1.5 in 2024 and 5 in the reported 2025 paper). SSC asks two-statement questions on the CPU, the units inside it, clock speed and cache, the size of an ASCII character, registers used in the instruction cycle, and address-line arithmetic such as how many lines a 4K x 8 memory needs. The section is qualifying, but a candidate for a Computer-Proficiency post needs a higher score, so every mark matters.

lines: A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data as input, processes it under the control of a stored program, stores it and gives the result as output.
The basic cycle is Input, Process, Output and Storage, often remembered as IPOS.
Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine and is called the father of the computer, while Ada Lovelace wrote the first published algorithm for his engine.
Five generations of computers are named after their switching technology: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors (VLSI) and artificial intelligence (ULSI).
The Central Processing Unit is the brain of the computer and has three parts: the Arithmetic Logic Unit, the Control Unit and the registers.
The ALU does arithmetic and logical comparisons, the Control Unit directs and coordinates every other unit, and registers are the fastest storage inside the CPU.
Cache memory sits between the CPU and RAM and is not one of the three basic units of the CPU, a point SSC tested in January 2025.
Every instruction passes through the machine cycle of fetch, decode, execute and store, and the clock speed in hertz sets how fast these steps run.
The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction and the Instruction Register holds the instruction being decoded and executed now.
Buses carry signals inside the computer: the address bus is one-way from the CPU, the data bus is two-way and the control bus carries timing and command signals.
The width of the address bus fixes how many memory locations can be reached, since n lines address 2 to the power n locations.
Computers store everything in binary, and a bit is one binary digit, a nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits.
Storage units rise in steps of 1024: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB and YB.
Character codes turn letters into numbers: ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters) and is stored in an 8-bit byte, EBCDIC uses 8 bits and Unicode covers every script.
Number system questions ask you to convert between binary (base 2), octal (base 8), decimal (base 10) and hexadecimal (base 16).
Computers are also classified by size into supercomputers, mainframes, minicomputers and microcomputers, and by data type into analog, digital and hybrid machines.

chapters.h: What a computer is and how it works
chapters.intro: SSC opens many papers with a simple definition question, so start with the words themselves. A computer takes raw data, processes it under a stored program and gives useful information. The stored-program idea, credited to John von Neumann, is why the same machine can run a word processor one minute and a game the next.

blocks.title: The IPOS cycle
steps: Input: data and instructions enter through devices such as the keyboard, mouse or scanner.
Processing: the CPU performs arithmetic and logical operations on the data.
Output: results leave through the monitor, printer or speakers.
Storage: data and results are kept in memory or on a disk for later use.

items.title: Information

blocks.title: Characteristics SSC lists
items: Speed: a computer works in microseconds, nanoseconds and picoseconds.
Accuracy: errors come from wrong input or programs, summed up as GIGO (garbage in, garbage out).
Diligence: a computer does not tire or lose concentration.
Versatility: one machine can do many different jobs.
Storage: it can hold and recall very large amounts of data.
No IQ: a computer cannot think or decide on its own without instructions.

chapters.intro: Generation questions ask which technology belonged to which generation, or which machine came first. Learn the switching device of each generation and the rest follows: smaller devices meant less heat, lower cost and higher speed.

items.what: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline, a mechanical adding machine.
Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine, which had a mill (processor) and a store (memory).
Ada Lovelace published notes with an algorithm for the Analytical Engine and is called the first programmer.
Herman Hollerith used punched cards for the US census, and his company later became IBM.
ENIAC, built by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, became the first general-purpose electronic digital computer.
UNIVAC I became the first commercially sold computer in the USA.
Intel released the 4004, the first single-chip microprocessor.
C-DAC, led by Vijay Bhatkar, built PARAM 8000, India's first supercomputer.

blocks.title: Indian firsts
blocks.body: TIFRAC, built at TIFR in 1960, was India's first indigenous computer, and Siddharth was the first Indian-made personal computer. PARAM 8000 of 1991 was the first Indian supercomputer, and the later PARAM series and the National Supercomputing Mission continue the line.

Personal use; desktops, laptops, tablets and smartphones

items.title: Analog
points: An analog computer works on continuously varying quantities.
Examples are the speedometer, thermometer and seismograph.

items.title: Digital
points: A digital computer works on discrete values, 0 and 1.
Examples are PCs, laptops and calculators.

items.title: Hybrid
points: A hybrid computer combines both types.
Examples are ICU patient monitors and petrol-pump dispensers.

blocks.title: By purpose
items: A general-purpose computer can run many kinds of programs, like a PC.
A special-purpose computer is built for one task, such as a traffic-light controller or the chip in a washing machine.
An embedded system is a special-purpose computer built inside another device, and it usually has a small fixed memory and a real-time operating system.

chapters.intro: SSC's favourite CPU items are two-statement questions. In January 2025 it said the CPU has three main units, the CU, the ALU and cache memory, and the correct answer was that this statement is false because the third unit is the register set, not the cache. Learn the exact three units.

blocks.title: Inside the CPU
rows: Adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides, and makes logical comparisons such as greater than, equal to and AND, OR, NOT
Fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals to memory, the ALU and I/O devices; it does not process data itself
Very small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the data and instructions in current use

blocks.title: Speed and performance
items: Clock speed is measured in hertz, and a 3 GHz CPU ticks three billion times a second, so clock speed controls the timing and pace of instruction execution.
Cache memory gives the CPU high-speed access to frequently used data and instructions, and the levels are L1 (smallest, fastest, inside each core), L2 and L3 (larger, often shared).
A multi-core processor has two or more cores on one chip, so it can run several tasks in parallel.
Word size is the number of bits the CPU handles at once, such as 32-bit or 64-bit.
Instructions per second are measured in MIPS, and floating-point speed in FLOPS.

items.title: Hardwired control unit
points: Control signals come from fixed logic circuits.
It is hard to change and is used in RISC processors.

items.title: Microprogrammed control unit
points: Control signals come from microinstructions stored in a control memory.
It is slower but flexible, because the design is changed by rewriting the microprogram.
It is used in CISC processors.

blocks.title: The brain versus the heart
blocks.body: The CPU is the brain of the computer, and the motherboard is the main circuit board that holds the CPU, RAM and slots. The ALU is sometimes called the heart of the CPU, but the Control Unit is called the nerve centre because it controls everything else.

chapters.intro: The reported 2025 paper asked which register holds the instruction being decoded and executed. The answer is the Instruction Register. Learn each register by the one job it does in the machine cycle.

blocks.title: Common CPU registers
rows: The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The instruction currently being decoded and executed
The address of the memory location being read or written
The data just read from, or about to be written to, memory
The address of the top of the stack
Condition bits such as zero, carry, sign and overflow

blocks.title: One pass of the machine cycle
steps: The address in the PC is copied into the MAR, and the PC is increased by one instruction.
Memory sends the instruction through the MDR into the IR.
The Control Unit decodes the instruction in the IR.
The ALU or another unit executes it, using the accumulator and other registers.
The result is stored in a register or written back to memory, and the cycle repeats.

blocks.title: Speed ladder
blocks.body: Registers are faster than cache, cache is faster than RAM, and RAM is faster than a hard disk. When an option asks for the fastest memory, choose registers. When it asks for the fastest memory outside the CPU core, choose cache.

chapters.intro: A bus is a set of parallel wires that carries signals between the CPU, memory and devices. The reported 2025 paper asked how many address lines a 4K x 8 memory needs, which is a two-line calculation once you know that n lines give 2 to the power n addresses.

blocks.title: The system bus
rows: The location in memory or the I/O port to be used
The actual data being read or written
Read, write, clock, interrupt and reset signals

items.f: Locations addressable = 2^n, where n = number of address lines
Address lines needed = log2(number of locations)
items.note: 4K = 4096 = 2^12, so a 4K x 8 memory needs 12 address lines.
In 4K x 8, the 8 is the word size, so it needs 8 data lines.

items.f: Memory size in bytes = locations x word length / 8

blocks.title: Do not multiply before taking the log
blocks.body: In 4K x 8, the address lines depend only on the 4K locations, not on 4K times 8. Taking log2 of 32K would give 15 lines, which is wrong.

chapters.intro: In January 2025 SSC asked the size of each ASCII character in bits and accepted 8 bits, because each character is stored in one byte. Learn the ladder of units and the four common codes.

blocks.title: Character codes
rows: American Standard Code for Information Interchange; A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48
Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code, used on IBM mainframes
Covers the world's scripts, including Devanagari

blocks.title: Byte ladder
blocks.key: King Midas Gave The Poor Every Zero Yet

chapters.intro: Number systems appear in CKT and in reasoning. The trick is to remember the base and the digits allowed, then use repeated division to go from decimal and place values to come back.

blocks.title: Converting
steps: Decimal to any base: divide repeatedly by the base and read the remainders from bottom to top; 25 in binary is 11001.
Any base to decimal: multiply each digit by the base raised to its position and add; 1011 in binary is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right; 110 101 is 65 in octal.
Binary to hexadecimal: group bits in fours from the right; 1010 1111 is AF in hexadecimal.
Fractions: multiply the fractional part by the base repeatedly and read the integer parts from top to bottom.

blocks.title: Complements and signs
items: The 1's complement of a binary number flips every bit, so 0101 becomes 1010.
The 2's complement is the 1's complement plus 1, and computers use it to store negative integers and to subtract by adding.
In a signed number, the leftmost bit is the sign bit, with 0 for positive and 1 for negative.
An n-bit unsigned number ranges from 0 to 2^n - 1, so one byte holds 0 to 255.

chapters.intro: Logic gates are the building blocks of the ALU. SSC rarely goes beyond the truth table of a single gate and the fact that NAND and NOR are universal gates.

blocks.title: Basic gates
rows: not all inputs are 1 (the opposite of AND)
all inputs are 0 (the opposite of OR)

blocks.title: Universal gates
blocks.body: NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any other gate, and so any digital circuit, can be built from only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

chapters.intro: The questions are short but worded carefully. Most errors come from reading a two-statement question too fast, so read every word of each statement against the facts above.

blocks.title: Patterns seen in 2023 to 2025
items: Two statements about the CPU are given, and you mark only 1, only 2, both or neither.
A True or False pair tests clock speed and cache.
A unit question asks the bits in an ASCII character, a nibble or a byte.
A register question asks which register holds the current instruction or the next address.
An address-bus question asks the number of lines for a given memory size.
A design question compares hardwired and microprogrammed control units.

blocks.title: Read the absolute words
blocks.body: Words such as only, always, never and all make a statement easy to test. If a statement says the CPU consists of the CU, ALU and cache memory, one wrong item makes the whole statement false.

formulas.f: Machine cycle = Fetch, Decode, Execute, Store
formulas.note: The PC points to the next instruction and the IR holds the current one.
Cache is not one of the three basic units.
n is the number of address lines.
One hex digit is one nibble.

formulas.f: ASCII = 7 bits (128 codes), stored in 1 byte
formulas.note: Extended ASCII uses all 8 bits for 256 codes.

formulas.f: Decimal value = Σ digit x base^position
formulas.note: Positions count from 0 at the right.

formulas.f: Speed ladder: registers > cache > RAM > SSD > HDD > tape
formulas.note: Cost per bit falls in the same order.

method: 1. Decide whether the question is about history, a CPU unit, a register, a bus, a data unit or a number conversion.
2. For a generation question, match the technology first: tubes, transistors, ICs, microprocessors, then AI.
3. For a CPU statement, check the three units (ALU, CU, registers) and reject any statement that swaps in cache or RAM.
4. For a register question, ask whether it wants the next address (PC), the current instruction (IR), a memory address (MAR) or data in transit (MDR).
5. For an address-bus question, write the number of locations as a power of 2 and read off the exponent.
6. For a data-unit question, remember 4, 8 and 1024, and that ASCII is 7-bit but stored in 8.
7. For a conversion, group bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal instead of going through decimal.
8. In two-statement questions, test each statement separately before looking at the options.
traps: Calling cache memory one of the three main units of the CPU is wrong, because the third unit is the register set.
Saying the Control Unit processes data is wrong, because it only directs the other units.
Mixing up the Program Counter and the Instruction Register is common: the PC holds the next address and the IR the current instruction.
Answering 7 bits for the size of an ASCII character loses marks when the question expects the stored size of 8 bits, as SSC's January 2025 key shows.
Taking 1 KB as 1000 bytes is wrong in the computer-memory sense, where 1 KB is 1024 bytes.
Multiplying the word length into the address-line calculation gives too many lines.
The address bus is one-way and the data bus is two-way, and swapping them is a classic slip.
Placing transistors in the first generation is wrong, because the first generation used vacuum tubes.
Calling ENIAC the first commercial computer is wrong, because that title belongs to UNIVAC I.
Calling the motherboard the brain is wrong, because the CPU is the brain.
Reading hexadecimal B as 12 is wrong, because A is 10, B is 11 and F is 15.
Treating NAND and NOR as ordinary gates misses their special status as universal gates.

examples.q: Which of the following statements about the Central Processing Unit (CPU) is/are correct? 1. The CPU is often referred to as the 'brain' of the computer. 2. The CPU consists of three main units: the control unit (CU), arithmetic logic unit (ALU), and cache memory. Options: Neither 1 nor 2, Only 2, Only 1, Both 1 and 2. (CGL 2024 Tier 2, 20 Jan 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Statement 1 is correct, because the CPU controls and processes everything and is called the brain. Step 2: Statement 2 is wrong, because the three basic units are the CU, the ALU and the registers, while cache is a separate fast memory. Step 3: Only statement 1 is correct.

examples.q: Select which statement(s) is/are True or False for the CPU. (i) The CPU's clock speed controls the timing and execution speed of instructions. (ii) The CPU's cache memory provides high-speed access to frequently used instructions and data. (CGL 2024 Tier 2, 18 Jan 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: The clock sets the pace of the fetch-decode-execute cycle, so (i) is true. Step 2: Cache holds recently and frequently used data close to the CPU, so (ii) is true. Step 3: Both are true.

examples.q: What is the size of each ASCII character in bits? Options: 4 bits, 16 bits, 8 bits, 5 bits. (CGL 2024 Tier 2, 20 Jan 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Standard ASCII defines 128 characters, which need 7 bits. Step 2: Each character is stored in one byte of 8 bits, with the extra bit used for parity or extended ASCII. Step 3: Of the options, 8 bits is correct, and 7 bits is not offered.

examples.q: A memory has a capacity of 4K x 8 bits. How many address lines are needed to identify every byte uniquely? (practice, modelled on the reported CGL 2025 paper)
examples.how: Step 1: 4K means 4 x 1024 = 4096 locations. Step 2: 4096 = 2^12. Step 3: So 12 address lines are needed, and the 8 gives the 8 data lines, not address lines.

examples.q: Which register holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed? (practice, modelled on the reported CGL 2025 paper)
examples.how: Step 1: The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction. Step 2: When the instruction is fetched, it is placed in the Instruction Register. Step 3: The Control Unit decodes it from the IR, so the answer is the IR.

examples.q: Convert the binary number 101101 to decimal, octal and hexadecimal. (practice)
examples.how: Step 1: Decimal: 32 + 0 + 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 45. Step 2: Octal: group in threes as 101 101, which is 5 and 5, so 55. Step 3: Hexadecimal: group in fours as 0010 1101, which is 2 and D, so 2D.

examples.q: Which generation of computers used integrated circuits? (practice)
examples.how: Step 1: The first used vacuum tubes and the second transistors. Step 2: Integrated circuits came in the third generation, from about 1964. Step 3: Microprocessors, which are very large ICs, define the fourth.

examples.q: What is the main advantage of a microprogrammed control unit over a hardwired one? (practice, modelled on the reported CGL 2025 paper)
examples.a: It is easier to modify, because control logic is stored as microinstructions
examples.how: Step 1: A hardwired unit uses fixed circuits and is fast but rigid. Step 2: A microprogrammed unit stores control steps in control memory. Step 3: Changing the microprogram changes the behaviour without redesigning hardware, so flexibility is the advantage.

examples.q: How many bytes are there in 2 MB? (practice)

revise: The CPU is the brain and has three units: the ALU, the CU and the registers.
Cache is fast memory between the CPU and RAM, with L1 the fastest and smallest.
Clock speed in GHz sets the pace of the fetch, decode, execute and store cycle.
The PC holds the next address, the IR the current instruction, the MAR a memory address and the MDR the data in transit.
The address bus is one-way, the data bus is two-way and the control bus carries commands.
n address lines reach 2^n locations, so 4K needs 12 lines.
A nibble is 4 bits, a byte is 8 bits and each step up from KB is 1024.
ASCII is 7-bit with 128 characters and is stored in 8 bits.
The generations run vacuum tubes, transistors, ICs, microprocessors and AI.
ENIAC (1946) was the first general-purpose electronic computer and UNIVAC I the first commercial one.
Babbage is the father of the computer and Ada Lovelace the first programmer.
PARAM 8000 (1991, C-DAC) was India's first supercomputer.
Hexadecimal uses 0 to 9 and A to F, and one hex digit equals 4 bits.
NAND and NOR are universal gates.
facts: History: Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulator was used in the 1890 US census.
History: the Intel 4004 of 1971 was a 4-bit microprocessor.
CPU: a 64-bit processor handles 64 bits in one operation.
CPU: GPUs have thousands of simple cores for parallel graphics and AI work.
Units: a word is the natural data size of a processor and is not fixed at 16 bits.
Codes: in ASCII, capital A is 65 and small a is 97, a difference of 32.
Classes: supercomputer speed is measured in FLOPS, and India's Pratyush and Mihir are used for weather forecasting.
Design: RISC processors, such as ARM chips in phones, use a small set of simple instructions.
